lessons.title: Cybersecurity Principles: CIA Triad
lessons.concept: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks, and data from attacks, damage, or unauthorized access. Core principles are the CIA triad: Confidentiality (prevent unauthorized disclosure), Integrity (prevent unauthorized modification), and Availability (ensure authorized access when needed).
lessons.formula: CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. Controls and practices aim to balance and maintain all three.
lessons.worked_example: Encryption supports confidentiality, checksums/digital signatures support integrity, and redundancy/backups support availability.
mistakes: Thinking cybersecurity is only about confidentiality
Ignoring availability as a security goal (e.g., DoS impacts availability)
Assuming one control solves all aspects

lessons.title: Common Threats and Attacks
lessons.concept: Common threats include malware (viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware), phishing (deceptive messages to steal info/credentials), brute-force/credential attacks, denial-of-service (DoS/DDoS), and SQL injection or other injection attacks against applications. Awareness and layered defenses reduce risk.
lessons.formula: Threat examples: phishing -> credential theft; ransomware -> encrypts data for ransom; DDoS -> overwhelms availability.
lessons.worked_example: A phishing email may impersonate a trusted entity and trick a user into revealing a password or clicking a malicious link.
mistakes: Assuming attacks are only technical (social engineering is common)
Believing antivirus alone prevents all threats
Underestimating weak passwords and unpatched systems

lessons.title: Basic Security Practices
lessons.concept: Good practices include strong unique passwords and multi-factor authentication (MFA), regular updates/patching, least privilege access, backups, encryption for sensitive data, secure configurations, and user awareness. Defense in depth uses multiple layers so failure of one control does not compromise everything.
lessons.formula: Practices: MFA, patching, least privilege, backups, encryption, monitoring, user training.
lessons.worked_example: MFA requires an additional factor (e.g., OTP/app approval) beyond password, reducing risk if password is stolen.
mistakes: Sharing passwords or reusing them across services

questions.question: Which security goal means data has not been altered in transit by an unauthorized party?
questions.explanation: Integrity guarantees accurate and unmodified data (often via hashes/HMAC). Confidentiality hides data (encryption), availability keeps services reachable, non-repudiation prevents denial of an action.

questions.question: Hashing a password with a unique random salt primarily protects against:
questions.explanation: A unique salt makes each stored hash unique even for identical passwords, so precomputed lookup tables (rainbow tables) and mass cracking of leaked hashes become infeasible.

questions.question: Which authentication factor is 'something you know'?
questions.explanation: The three classic factors are knowledge (password/PIN), possession (token/card/phone) and inherence (biometrics such as fingerprint or retina). A password is a knowledge factor.
